notes: Sample emergency_operations.json - how hard each dangerous operation is to authorise. Copy to emergency_operations.json and edit.

This is deliberately NOT the chat clearance file. telegram_support_commands.json says WHO may ask for an operation; this says HOW HARD it is to confirm once asked. The two carry the same number for the same operation and a test pins that they agree, but they answer different questions - and the shared operations layer reads no chat settings at all, which is what lets the same confirmation apply to a shell caller, a scheduled run and a chat message.

'confirmations' is how many separate answers the caller must give. 'challenge': 'target_id' makes the second answer the target's own identifier, typed out. That cannot be given from muscle memory - it has to be read off the prompt - and a payload written for one host is then rejected by another.
'effects' is written for the person at the prompt at 3am. It is the sentence they read before typing yes, so it says what actually happens, not what the command is called.
An operation not listed here has no entry and therefore no confirmation. Add the entry in the same change that adds the operation.

100.note: Takes a machine or a service down. Two answers: 'yes', then the target's own id typed out.

50.note: No downtime, but a large blast radius: rolls back a transaction, moves a file, starts work on a production instance. One typed 'yes'.
